Match day report · Week 8, Day 2

Latest session

Anto + Jothi Sai won W8 D2, beating Pawan + John 21–17 in the final. Pawan topped the qualifier and went in as seed 1. Best adjusted day: Pawan (+4.85 per match once partners and opponents are taken out, 3–2); best record: Anto (6–1, +36). Biggest win: Anto + Pawan 21–2 over Pratap + Bhanu.

How to read this report. Every figure is marked Measured (counted straight from the match records) or Estimate (from a statistical model, with its uncertainty). Pairings in this league are deliberately balanced, strong with weak, so raw win rates are pulled toward even and partner records reflect the draw. The adjusted estimates correct for that. A single match is noisy: after accounting for who is on court, margins still vary by about — points, so only the larger differences here are reliable.

Partnership analysis

Partnerships here are assigned, not chosen: the workbook builds balanced teams from its ratings, so strong players are usually paired with weak ones. That makes a raw partnership record mostly a measure of the two players’ combined strength. To find genuine chemistry, each pair’s results are compared with what the two players’ separate estimates predict against the opponents they actually met. Out of — partnerships, — differs from expectation by more than chance would usually allow — no more than chance alone would produce across that many pairs. In short, there is no reliable evidence of special chemistry or clashes; partnership results are explained by individual strength.

Opponent analysis

In doubles each match puts a player against two opponents at once, and every opponent also had a partner, so a head-to-head record is shared credit. Records against the strongest players are poor for everyone simply because those players are strong. The useful question is whether anyone does unusually well or badly against a particular opponent once strength is accounted for. The answer is no: across all pairings with — or more meetings, the largest such deviation is — points per match, within normal match-to-match noise. There are no hidden “bogey” matchups in this data.

Advanced statistical analysis

Adjusted strength with 90% intervals

Estimate

Points per match each player adds to a team’s margin versus an average player. Solid: whole season. Hollow: recency-weighted.

Chance of each final rank

Estimate

From — resamples of whole session days. Expected wins use out-of-sample predictions for every match.

Elo rating through the season

Estimate

Margin-weighted Elo after each session day. Everyone starts at —.

Workbook rating by day

Measured

The — rating the workbook used to make the draw each day. Blank: did not play.

Season ranking progression

Measured

Rank on cumulative points difference after each day.

Method

Estimate
  1. Adjusted plus-minus (ridge regression). Each match is one equation: team A’s margin = the two A players’ values − the two B players’ values + noise. Solving all — equations together separates each player from partners and opponents. A small ridge penalty (λ = —, chosen by leaving out one day at a time) keeps estimates stable; values sum to zero, so an estimate of one point means a player adds one point per match more than the average of these — players.
  2. Uncertainty. Whole session days were resampled with replacement — times and the model refitted each time; the middle — of refits gives each interval and the rank probabilities.
  3. Form and change. A recency-weighted fit (weights halve every — session days) estimates current level. Separate fits of the first — and last — days estimate change. Daily adjusted performance — each day’s margins minus what partners and opponents predict — feeds the trend and consistency figures.
  4. Elo. Each player starts at —. A team’s rating is the average of its two players; after each match both winners gain and both losers lose — × (result − expected), scaled up for wider margins. Elo depends on match order and needs time to settle, so it is a progression view, not the main estimate.
  5. Expectations. A predicted margin and the model’s leftover spread (— points) give each team’s chance of winning. Predictions used for expected wins come from fits that leave out the day being predicted.

How well it works, and its limits

Estimate
  • Validation. Predicting each day from the other —, the model’s average margin error is — points against — for a no-information guess, and it names the winner — of the time. It explains about — of the variation in margins; the rest is ordinary match-to-match variation. Elo picked — of winners from W1 D4 on.
  • The workbook’s own rating uses the same kind of fit and reports a similar error, and its fitted values (Season tab, to W7 D2) agree with this model that Anto (—) is ahead of Jothi Sai (—); this model has Anto first in — of resamples. The scoring app’s latest refit (used for W8 D2) differs on the whole-number scale in three ways: it puts John level with Anto at 5, although the season estimates are — points per match apart; it drops Jothi Sai to 4, below John, although Jothi Sai is ahead on both the season and recency-weighted fits; and it rates Dinesh above Pawan, which neither the season fit nor the recency-weighted fit supports (recent: Dinesh —, Pawan —).
  • Additive assumption. The model treats a pair as the sum of two players. The partnership tab checks for chemistry directly and finds none beyond chance.
  • Constant ability. The season estimate assumes a player’s level is fixed; the recency and half-season fits relax that.
  • No rally data. Only final scores exist, so nothing here says anything about technique, fitness or tactics.
  • Small samples. Players have —–— matches. Season estimates are good to about — points; pair and head-to-head figures are much less certain.

  1. Day 1 final incomplete. Only the first game (Pratap + Jothi Sai —) was recorded; the decider was not. The Season tab counts that game as the title and as a final. Jothi Sai’s titles are — counted, — confirmed; Pratap’s — counted, — confirmed.
  2. Impossible scores. — appears — times: W3 D2 round 6, W6 D1 round 5 and the W6 D1 final. The W3 D2 note calls it “a two-point lead”, which it is not. Each is used as recorded; the effect is at most one point per match.
  3. Days not in the workbook’s totals. The All matches tab stops at W7 D2. W7 D3 has its own tab with every score but is not counted by the Season tab. W8 D1, W8 D2 are not in the workbook at all: the scores were entered from the scoring app into extra-days.json. This report counts all of them, so its totals run 26 matches ahead of the Season tab until the workbook catches up.
  4. No starting rating for Dinesh. Dinesh missed W1 D1 and W1 D2; the first rating (—) is from W1 D3.
  5. Unequal attendance and weeks. Matches per player range from — to —, and weeks run — days. All comparisons use per-match rates.
  6. Knockout formats changed several times (one eliminator, three eliminators, recount qualification, on W7 D3 a five-player format with seed 1 going straight to the final, and on W8 D2 a seven-player format with seed 1 straight to the final and three eliminators counted on a recount for the other three places). Eliminator wins do not always equal qualification for the final.
  7. Non-random pairings. The draw is built from ratings to balance teams. Raw partner and opponent records are therefore confounded by the draw, which is why the adjusted model is used.
  8. Unsigned projections. The workbook’s “Projected margin” column (from W2 D3, qualifier rounds only) gives size but not direction, so it cannot be checked against results.
  9. Leftover template text. Several played tabs still say “Fill in the YELLOW score cells only”, and W1 D5 carries a planning note about projected rounds. Cosmetic only.

Day labels: W1 D1–W1 D5 are the workbook tabs “Day 1”–“Day 5”; later tabs keep their own names.
